doc.title: Joe Temperley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997

title: Moving to a Glasgow nightclub and learning from Jimmy Morgan
summary: His first club job in Glasgow was traumatic for a country boy; trumpeter Jimmy Morgan taught him about music.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the horn: first instrument and the trombone

blocks.x: At what point in your early years as a saxophonist did you make a conscious decision that you were going to make a living as a musician?

No it just sort of grew on me I guess. When I first started off in Scotland, I went to work in a nightclub in Glasgow. And that was a traumatic experience for me, even though I was only moving 50 miles from my home town, my accent for instance was completely different from a Glasgow accent. I was a real country bumpkin.

Well the accents in the British Isles are very regional. You know you can, even in London there’s about four or five completely different accents you know. North London is completely different from South London. And I mean you wouldn’t really sort of think about that until you actually live there and you can hear the difference. And this, in Scotland, when I went to Glasgow, that was a big traumatic experience for me. And I started playing little bits of jazz and going to jazz clubs and I had a gig in a night club with a five piece band and there was a trumpet player, his name was Jimmy Morgan, and he had come up from London. He’d been living in London for a long time. And I learned a lot of stuff from him, talking about music and talking about playing and this is how you do this and that. I learned a lot. And that’s how, in those days, that’s how you came to gain knowledge, by listening to other people and actually experiencing it for yourself. Nowadays I teach at the Manhattan School of Music. And it’s a whole different thing. The kids today are in danger of maybe of learning too much too fast. And it sort of homogenizes the playing. It tends to make them sound like the same.
